source.title: Streaming CTR Prediction: Rethinking Recommendation Task for Real-World Streaming Data
source.authors: Qiwen Wang; Hongyu Lu; Yu Chen; Da-Wei Zhou; De-Chuan Zhan; Ming Chen; Han-Jia Ye

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; figures and some tables are flattened, but the text and several table values are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures CTR performance under streaming distribution shift. It does not test the listed claims about same-distribution generalization, random-label memorization, or the specified model and benchmark settings.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on model size, normalization, dropout, regularization, optimizer, batch size, and training epochs. These concern static CTR performance and streaming or out-of-distribution performance, so they do not test the claim versions as stated. Some figure-only trends are described in text but lack recoverable exact values.
record.test_reason: The dropout experiment bears on V6 in a new setting: an embedding-plus-fully-connected binary classifier on Avazu. CTR prediction is a classification task, and pAUC measures held-out performance on an i.i.d. split. The record incorrectly excludes this experiment merely because it concerns CTR. The other experiments do not establish the conditions required by the remaining versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors define a streaming CTR benchmark, report that some factors affect static and streaming performance differently, and improve baselines through selected hyperparameter changes and exemplar replay. They explicitly caution that their qualitative findings may not apply across all CTR architectures.
record.recipe_differences: Studies CTR prediction on Avazu with a pretraining stage followed by streaming updates and distribution-shift evaluation; the claim versions concern other tasks or same-distribution generalization.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported performance varies with embedding dimension, MLP depth and width, normalization, dropout, regularization, optimizer, batch size, and number of streaming training epochs. The paper notes that optimal steps for current and online AUC often differ.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing embedding size, MLP depth, and MLP width affects static, online, and future-distribution AUC differently, without establishing an interpolation threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capacity changes can have different benefits for static and streaming CTR prediction.

fits_no_version.finding: CTR AUC increases and then saturates with batch size; static and online optima can differ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The batch size preferred for static CTR prediction can differ from that preferred for streaming prediction.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalization and separate embedding or MLP regularization interventions produce different static and streaming performance patterns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization and regularization choices for CTR models should be evaluated against their deployment distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam obtains higher static and online AUC than SGD in the reported CTR comparison; AdamW has similar performance to Adam.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the reported default protocol, Adam-based optimization performs well for streaming CTR prediction.

record.problems: The authors say the diverse CTR model structures may make some factor conclusions inapplicable across structures. Several factor trends are figure-only, and the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the extracted values.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only parameter-size trends, normalization-parameter ablations, and training-epoch plots were not extracted as separate rows because exact condition values or metrics are not reliably recoverable from the flattened figures. Table 14 improvement-method results are outside the claim versions and are not included.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-versus-random-label held-out performance.
Width increases beyond an established zero-training-error threshold in converged, unregularized networks.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, local connectivity, and transferred initialization.
Adaptive-versus-SGD generalization on image or language benchmarks under the specified tuning regimes and recovery interventions.
Large-batch penalties on image or language workloads under controlled epoch budgets and their recovery through recipe changes.

Classification error at a fixed decision rule; very small training sets; convolutional classifiers; training measurements establishing underfitting; and joint dropout/weight-decay removal with data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, generalization gaps, and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures.
Identification and removal of memorized examples versus equal-sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V6. R5's reversed state describes the measured dropout-versus-zero-dropout direction; the verdict is limits_scope because V6 asserts benefits only in some regimes. No training/test generalization gap is required to evaluate a held-out-performance intervention.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label test performance.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU sweep beyond the zero-training-error threshold on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison.
Optimizer comparisons are on CTR models in the paper's static and streaming settings, not the stated image-classification or language benchmarks.
Batch size is studied for CTR models under streaming and static settings, not the stated image-classification or language benchmarks.
Dropout is measured in CTR models, not the stated fully connected and convolutional classifier regimes; no joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or norm- and margin-based generalization-measure comparison.
No memorized-example identification, removal, or retraining comparison.

Online and frozen-model future-distribution AUC also decline. AUC measures ranking performance; these results do not directly establish classification-error changes or underfitting.

relationships.condition: Avazu embedding-plus-MLP classifier, dropout rates 0.5 and 0.9 versus zero dropout
relationships.reason: R5 shows lower static held-out pAUC at both dropout rates, with corresponding declines in online and future-distribution AUC. This identifies an additional regime where dropout harms held-out performance; it does not refute benefits in other regimes.
relationships.display_finding: Both dropout rates lowered AUC on a fixed held-out dataset, in online evaluation and on data from a future distribution. These AUC results did not establish changes in classification error.
